text: From Descartes to the present. <break time="0.8s" /> Reason has been prized in Western culture. <break time="0.8s" /> Standing as the chief virtue of the modernist world view. <break time="0.8s" /> As we are led to believe. <break time="0.8s" /> It is the power to reason. <break time="0.8s" /> That sets humans above the remainder of the animal kingdom. <break time="0.8s" /> And is essential for human survival. <break time="0.8s" /> Literary study suggests otherwise. <break time="0.8s" /> Among the most important objections. <break time="0.8s" /> Are those of the French literary theorist Jacques Derrida. <break time="0.8s" /> Derridas writings. <break time="0.8s" /> Often identified as deconstructionist. <break time="0.8s" /> Are ambiguous and open to many interpretations. <break time="0.8s" /> From one perspective, however. <break time="0.8s" /> They significantly undermine. <break time="0.8s" /> The cultural investment in human reason. <break time="0.8s" /> Consider two major premises. <break time="0.8s" /> First, suggests Derrida. <break time="0.8s" /> Rational arguments bring about a massive suppression of meaning. <break time="0.8s" /> Broadly put. <break time="0.8s" /> When we are convinced by a rational argument. <break time="0.8s" /> We do not know more. <break time="0.8s" /> But less. <break time="0.8s" /> Second if closely examined. <break time="0.8s" /> All rational arguments will collapse. <break time="0.8s" /> Rationality, then. <break time="0.8s" /> Is not a foundation for anything. <break time="0.8s" /> For our institutions of government and science, for example. <break time="0.8s" /> Or as a way of deciding. <break time="0.8s" /> On what is moral or worthwhile. <break time="0.8s" /> Rather, Derrida suggests. <break time="0.8s" /> Our good reasons are in the end. <break time="0.8s" /> Both suppressive and empty.
